title: Launch Now or Wait to Rearm
location: Flag bridge of the aircraft carrier Akagi, roughly 200-240 nautical miles northwest of Midway Atoll, Pacific Ocean
t0: Aboard Akagi on the morning of June 4, 1942, Vice Admiral Nagumo has to decide whether to launch an immediate strike with whatever aircraft are ready -- a mix of planes still armed for a second Midway land-strike and others partway through rearming -- or to recover the returning first Midway strike wave, complete a uniform rearming with anti-ship ordnance, and launch one fully coordinated, fighter-escorted strike later that morning. The window opens with the first ambiguous scout report at 0728 and closes once Nagumo commits to the recover-and-rearm plan around 0830-0837.
context_summary: A Japanese scout plane has just reported enemy ships -- possibly with a carrier among them -- while Nagumo's own strike aircraft are only partly rearmed and his first Midway wave is still inbound and low on fuel. Standing doctrine calls for one full, coordinated strike. Waiting for it means leaving the fleet exposed for two more hours while the enemy carrier's exact position stays unconfirmed.
immediate_outcome: Nagumo ordered the returning Midway strike wave recovered first and organized a coordinated strike for a target launch around 1030. Before that strike could be launched, US Navy Dauntless dive bombers from Enterprise and Yorktown attacked Kido Butai at approximately 1020-1026, finding Akagi, Kaga, and Soryu with little fighter cover at altitude; all three were left ablaze within about six minutes. The fourth carrier, Hiryu, launched counterstrikes that critically damaged Yorktown before Hiryu herself was located and sunk later that day. Japan lost all four fleet carriers of Kido Butai and a large share of its trained carrier aircrew and deck/maintenance personnel.
long_term_outcome: The loss of four fleet carriers and their trained air groups in a single day ended Japan's capacity to conduct offensive carrier operations at the scale of the war's first six months, and the battle is conventionally described by historians as the turning point of the Pacific naval war, though its causal weight relative to other factors (US industrial output, later campaigns) is itself debated. Modern primary-source research (Parshall & Tully, 'Shattered Sword', 2005) also argues that the popular postwar image of Japanese flight decks packed with fully armed, fueled aircraft at the moment of the American attack -- traceable mainly to Mitsuo Fuchida's 1955 memoir -- is not well supported by surviving Japanese action reports, and that the American attack's success depended substantially on an independent chain of decisions on the US side.

options.label: Launch immediately with whatever aircraft are ready
options.short_description: Order an immediate scratch strike using the aircraft already on or near the flight deck -- a mix of some still carrying land-attack bombs and others partway through rearming with torpedoes -- launched with minimal fighter escort and without waiting to recover the incoming Midway strike wave.
options.upside: Could put ordnance in the air against the reported enemy force well before 1030, closing the window during which the American carrier, once confirmed, might find and strike Kido Butai first.
options.downside: A hastily assembled, mixed-ordnance strike with little or no fighter escort risked heavy losses to American carrier fighters and had less concentrated striking power against an armored flight deck, while the fuel-critical Midway strike wave would be left to circle or ditch.
known_tradeoffs: Could put ordnance in the air against the reported enemy force well before 1030, closing the window during which the American carrier, once confirmed, might find and strike Kido Butai first. versus A hastily assembled, mixed-ordnance strike with little or no fighter escort risked heavy losses to American carrier fighters and had less concentrated striking power against an armored flight deck, while the fuel-critical Midway strike wave would be left to circle or ditch.

options.label: Recover the Midway wave, complete rearming, launch one coordinated strike
options.short_description: Land the returning first Midway strike wave, finish a uniform rearming of the reserve aircraft with torpedoes and anti-ship bombs, assemble a full fighter escort, and launch a single concentrated strike against the American force once its position and composition were confirmed, targeted for roughly 1030.
options.upside: A properly escorted, uniformly armed strike at full strength had the best chance of inflicting decisive damage on an American carrier in one blow, and matched standing Imperial Japanese Navy doctrine for how a carrier strike should be conducted.
options.downside: Bought the American side roughly two more hours in which to locate Kido Butai and strike first, and kept Japanese flight decks occupied with recovery, rearming, and spotting operations throughout that window.
known_tradeoffs: A properly escorted, uniformly armed strike at full strength had the best chance of inflicting decisive damage on an American carrier in one blow, and matched standing Imperial Japanese Navy doctrine for how a carrier strike should be conducted. versus Bought the American side roughly two more hours in which to locate Kido Butai and strike first, and kept Japanese flight decks occupied with recovery, rearming, and spotting operations throughout that window.

case_information.content: At 0715, before any enemy ships had been reported, Nagumo ordered the reserve strike aircraft -- which had been held armed with torpedoes and armor-piercing bombs for a possible anti-ship mission -- rearmed with high-explosive bombs for a second strike on Midway's land facilities, based on reports from the returning first wave that a second attack on the atoll was needed.
At 0728, a scout floatplane launched from the cruiser Tone reported sighting what appeared to be ten enemy surface ships roughly 240 miles from Midway, without specifying ship types.

A follow-up report around 0809 described the contact as cruisers and destroyers, which did not by itself indicate a carrier was present; only at approximately 0820 did the same scout amend the report to say the force was accompanied by what appeared to be an aircraft carrier.

Rearming aircraft from one ordnance type to another was slow, manual work: torpedoes and bombs had to be winched down and moved by hand-cranked trucks, of which each carrier had only a limited number, so only a handful of aircraft could be rearmed at any one time and the process could not be quickly reversed once underway.

The first Midway strike wave, launched at dawn, was returning low on fuel and needed to land; most of Kido Butai's fighters were either escorting that wave, flying combat air patrol over the fleet, or being recycled through both duties, leaving few fighters free to escort an immediate scratch strike.

Imperial Japanese Navy carrier doctrine at the time emphasized launching full, uniformly armed, fighter-escorted strikes rather than piecemeal attacks, on the reasoning that a small or uncoordinated strike against a defended target risked heavy losses for little result.

Rear Admiral Tamon Yamaguchi, commanding Carrier Division 2 from the Hiryu, signaled a recommendation that Nagumo launch a strike immediately with the aircraft that were ready, rather than wait for a fully coordinated force.

Three US carriers -- Enterprise, Hornet, and Yorktown -- were present and operating against Kido Butai, not one or two as Japanese pre-battle intelligence had assumed; Yorktown, believed by Japan to have been sunk or put out of action at the Battle of the Coral Sea a month earlier, had in fact been patched up at Pearl Harbor in roughly 72 hours and sailed in time to take part.

US dive bombers from Enterprise and Yorktown were already airborne and searching for Kido Butai during the period Nagumo was weighing his options; their eventual attack, which arrived at approximately 1020, resulted substantially from an independent chain of decisions on the American side rather than from anything Nagumo did or did not do in this specific window.

According to Jonathan Parshall and Anthony Tully's primary-source reconstruction in 'Shattered Sword' (2005), the popular postwar account of Japanese flight decks packed with fully armed, fueled aircraft at the moment of the American attack -- largely traceable to Mitsuo Fuchida's 1955 memoir -- is not well supported by surviving Japanese action reports and deck-cycle records; Akagi in particular likely had few if any strike aircraft actually spotted on her flight deck at 1020.

How much weight this specific decision carried for the battle's ultimate outcome, relative to earlier doctrinal choices and to essentially independent events on the American side, remains a matter of ongoing historical interpretation, not something Nagumo could have assessed at the time.

evidence.title: Shattered Sword: The Untold Story of the Battle of Midway
evidence.citation: Parshall, J. & Tully, A. (2005). Shattered Sword: The Untold Story of the Battle of Midway. Potomac Books.
evidence.supported_claim: Primary-source reconstruction of the 0715 rearming order, the 0728/0809/0820 scout reports, IJN deckload-strike doctrine, the state of Kido Butai's flight decks at 1020, and the argument that the American attack's success depended substantially on an independent chain of US decisions.

evidence.title: Midway: The Battle that Doomed Japan, the Japanese Navy's Story
evidence.citation: Fuchida, M. & Okumiya, M. (1955). Midway: The Battle that Doomed Japan. United States Naval Institute Press.
evidence.supported_claim: Fuchida's own postwar account of the battle, including his description of Kido Butai's flight decks at the moment of the American attack, which established the popular 'five fateful minutes' narrative later disputed by Shattered Sword.
